title: The till is out
text: At close, the drawer is forty dollars short. The manager is counting it a second time with a face like a locked door, and you were the last one on it.

choices.label: Count it with them, out loud

outcomes.text: We found a pair of stuck notes under the tray. Forty dollars, and a lot of unearned suspicion lifted.
The count stayed short. They wrote it up as an error and nobody said my name, which is its own kind of looking.
I put two twenties in. It was a stupid, noble thing. They gave it back the next week.
I paid it. They never gave it back, and I never forgot.
It sorted itself out by morning. It had never been mine to fix.
They remembered I'd said nothing. It was held against me, quietly, at the next rota.

title: A customer with a coupon
text: A man holds up the line over a coupon that expired yesterday. The queue behind him is getting loud. He is not wrong, exactly. He is just very loud.

outcomes.text: He left with an expression of astonished gratitude. The queue forgave me instantly.
Next day the manager docked it from the till. 'Policy.' I should have known.
He stormed out. A woman behind him said 'thank you' with her eyes.
He asked for a manager. The manager sided with him. I stood there and learned how it works.

choices.label: Call the supervisor and step back

outcomes.text: It was resolved in thirty seconds by somebody paid more to deal with it. A lesson in itself.
The supervisor took forty minutes. The queue was a fire.

title: Grease fire
text: The fryer flares up with a roar and a wall of orange. Everyone freezes for one stupid second. You are the closest person to the red extinguisher.

outcomes.text: Foam everywhere, and out in four seconds. The manager called me 'a natural' and meant it.
I got it out and burned the back of my hand. A scar the shape of a small country.

choices.label: Hit the kill switch and shout

outcomes.text: Everyone got out in time. Nobody was hurt. I got a free lunch for a month.
The flare caught the hood vent. The kitchen closed for a day.
It was a small fire and everyone saw me leave. The nickname lasted a year.
Somebody else put it out. They did not say a word to me for a week, which was worse than saying it.

title: Mystery shopper
text: A woman orders a plain burger and spends eleven minutes writing in a small notebook. The manager has gone pale. 'That's corporate,' he whispers, to nobody.

outcomes.text: I topped up her drink, wiped her table, and learned her name. The report said 'exceptional'. It came with a voucher.
I was so bright and eager I forgot a customer's order. The notebook caught it.
I made her burger like I make everyone's. It scored well enough, and the manager hugged me, which was bad.
It was a middling score and a long conversation about 'consistency'.

choices.label: Spot her and tell the whole shift

outcomes.text: The place had never been so clean. We all got a pizza afterwards and nobody mentioned how.
The manager made us stand in a row and be silent. It was the weirdest shift of my life.

title: A kid goes under
text: From the chair it is simply a pair of flailing arms between a thousand others, and then it is not. You are already moving before you decide to move.

outcomes.text: I had her up and on the deck in twenty seconds. She coughed, cried, and then asked for ice cream. Her mother hugged me for a long time.
I got her out, but the water had her and she needed an ambulance. She was fine. I was not, for a week.

choices.label: Blow the whistle and use the pole

outcomes.text: The pole reached. It was the right call and the training manual's exact words. She was fine.
The pole was just short. A father got there first. I couldn't look at him after.
It took an extra five seconds that felt like an hour. She was fine. I replayed those seconds every night.
Someone else was already in the water. I never learned if they were faster than I'd have been.

title: Heat and a bad shift
text: Thirty-eight degrees and a full pool. Your whistle hand has gone numb and your vision has started to swim at the edges.

outcomes.text: They swapped me and I sat in the shade with a bottle of water for ten minutes. A small mercy.
They told me to 'tough it out'. I did, and I'd resent them for it later.
I stayed on the chair until close. I could barely walk to the bus.
I nearly fainted, and a kid saw it. The manager sent me home early, apologetic.

choices.label: Pour water over my head and keep going

outcomes.text: It worked for about twenty minutes. I felt like a legend.
It worked for about twenty minutes.

title: The wrong kind of quiet
text: The kids went to bed an hour ago and it has been far too silent for far too long. You stand at the bottom of the stairs, listening.

outcomes.text: Both asleep, one still gripping a torch. Heartbreakingly sweet.
The five-year-old was awake and had drawn all over the landing wall. In crayon, not pen, thank God.
They laughed and said 'that means they're asleep'. Mildly insulting.
They came home early and weren't happy. I didn't get a tip.
It was fine. I got to watch my show in peace. A good night's work.
It was not fine. I woke to a child standing next to me, saying one word: 'hungry'.

title: A fever at nine pm
text: The little one is hot to the touch, flushed, and crying in a way that is not tantrum-crying. Their mother's phone goes straight to voicemail.

outcomes.text: They talked me through it. A fever, and a good, slow calm. When the parents came home I was practically a hero.
The ambulance came for a childhood fever and a parent was annoyed. I was told I'd done the right thing anyway.

choices.label: Cool them down and keep trying the parents

outcomes.text: I did what I'd read. It broke by midnight. The mother cried when she hugged me.
It held. They came home to a quiet house, and I never found out how close it had been.
I called my own mother and we sorted it out over the phone. Not my best moment. Not my worst.
I cried too. It's a feeling I understand differently now.

title: Six leads, one squirrel
text: You have six dogs on six leads, and every one of them has just seen the same squirrel. The leads wrap you like a maypole.

outcomes.text: I held. I was dragged six metres but I held. The dogs looked at me with new respect.
I held and fell. A very kind woman helped me up and I never knew her name.
The loose one came back in a minute, delighted. I got the lecture from its owner anyway.
It did not come back for four terrifying hours.
They ran in a happy bundle straight into the tennis club. Chaos, and a story I'll tell forever.
The park keeper had to catch them with a coat. He was furious.

title: The dog who knows
text: One of your regulars, an elderly spaniel, always pulls to the same bench. Today you let it, and an old man sitting there says, 'She was his.'

outcomes.text: He told me about the dog's owner, his wife, and the walks they used to take. I came away very quiet and very glad.
He started to cry gently. We sat there a long time.
I felt that I'd missed something. I took a different route next time and sat on that bench myself.
The next week he wasn't there.
The owner's voice changed. It turned out to be a bigger story than I'd guessed, and a lovely one.
The owner told me to mind my own business. It was fair.

title: The student who stares
text: Your student has been looking at the same maths problem for twelve minutes without writing a thing. His mother is pacing in the next room, pretending not to listen.

outcomes.text: He admitted he didn't understand any of it, and hadn't for months. We started again from the beginning. It was the best hour of the year.
He went quiet, then shrugged. Something loosened a bit.

choices.label: Show the solution and move on

outcomes.text: He copied it down. He passed the test, and learned nothing.
His mother saw the page and was delighted. She doubled my pay. I felt like a fraud.
We turned it into a points race. He beat me, fairly. Next week he asked for harder ones.
It worked for ten minutes and then he got bored. But he laughed, which was new.

title: Exam night
text: It's the night before her exam and her mother has called you in a panic. 'Can you come tonight? I'll pay double.'

outcomes.text: We went through every past paper at the kitchen table. She got a B+. Her mum wept with joy.
She sat the exam exhausted. I wasn't sure it had been a good idea.

choices.label: Say no, kindly, and send a one-page summary

outcomes.text: It was the better idea. She slept, and passed.
Her mum was cross, but the summary helped.

choices.label: Turn up and chat, not teach

outcomes.text: I told her she already knew it all. She believed me. She was right.
She was calmer. It didn't help the exam, but it helped her.

title: The ten-person order
text: A man walks in, tablet in hand, and reads out a ten-drink order with modifiers. Behind him, a queue to the door.

outcomes.text: I got every one right. He actually clapped.
I got nine right and one wrong. He tipped anyway.

choices.label: Ask a coworker to share the load

outcomes.text: We were a machine. The queue melted. It was weirdly beautiful.
My coworker sighed theatrically. We got it done.
Two drinks came out cold and one with the wrong milk. He complained. The manager sided with him.
He was nice about it. I wasn't.

title: The regular who never smiles
text: A man in a grey coat comes in at 7:12 every morning and orders a flat white without a word. Today he says, 'You remember my order. Thank you.'

outcomes.text: He's a widower, it turned out. He had never been asked. I learned his name, and every morning thereafter I had it ready.
He said 'fine' and looked at the floor. He didn't come in for a week, then did.
He nodded and left. It was a tiny thing and I never knew if it mattered.
The next day he asked for a different coffee and I got it wrong. We both laughed.

choices.label: Write his name on the cup

outcomes.text: He looked at the cup for a long moment. He kept it.
He frowned, then smiled, then took a different seat. I think it was shyness.

title: The pallet jack
text: The pallet jack's brake has been sticky all week. On aisle nine, loaded with tinned tomatoes, it begins to roll.

choices.label: Throw yourself in front of it

outcomes.text: It stopped against my knees. I limped for a week and was a hero for a day.
My shin was bruised blue and I was told off for not following protocol. The irony stayed with me.
It crashed into the end shelf and sixty tins went rolling. No one was hurt.
It hit a display of cereal. We were laughing by closing time.

choices.label: Grab the handle and yank the brake

outcomes.text: It bit, just in time. I felt like a stunt person.
The brake snapped off. I held the handle like an idiot while it rolled.

title: Nightshift, 3 a.m.
text: The store is silent except for the buzz of a light that has been flickering for an hour. Something in the back freezer has begun to knock.

outcomes.text: It was a loose crate, knocking in a draught. I laughed out loud, alone, at 3 a.m. Good.
It was a fox, which had been sleeping in the loading bay. We eyed each other. It left.
Nothing on the footage. I never solved it.
The footage showed a trolley, rolling by itself on a slope. Case closed.
The knocking stopped. I decided that was the right call.
It went on for the rest of the shift. I was relieved when the day crew arrived.

title: The wrong address
text: The app says to drop the order at number 14. Number 14 is a boarded-up house with a dog behind the fence, and the customer is texting: 'Where ARE you?'

outcomes.text: It was 41, not 14, the app had swapped the digits. A big tip for the trouble.
They didn't answer. I cancelled and ate their curry myself in the car.
The dog and I came to an understanding. The neighbour took the food. I never knew if she was the customer.
The dog did not come to an understanding.
They reported it as missing. The platform sided with them.
The neighbour's cat ate the starter. It was all anyone talked about.

title: Pouring rain, two orders
text: It is the heaviest rain of the year, and the orders are stacking up. One more run, and your hands are shaking from the cold.

outcomes.text: I got soaked, but the tips were generous. It paid for the week.
I skidded at a roundabout and lost a whole order into a gutter.

choices.label: Take one, wait out the worst

outcomes.text: I sat in a bus shelter and watched the rain, quietly satisfied.
The second order was given to someone else and I lost the tip.
Dry, warm, and a little ashamed. It was the right call.
The platform noted my low acceptance rate. It cost me.

title: The returns desk
text: A woman puts a sofa cushion on your counter. It has clearly been used, and the box it came in has clearly never been near it. 'I want a refund,' she says, with her whole chest.

outcomes.text: She called me names and then called the manager. The manager took my side, which is rare and I valued it.
She returned with a camera crew. It turned out to be her nephew. We all moved on.
She got her money and left, smiling. I was told off for it later.
She came back the next week with a different cushion. I stood my ground that time.
He did the little speech. She did the little speech. They bowed to each other like wrestlers. I learned a lot.
The manager gave her store credit. She left happier than anyone should be.

title: The last week before the holiday
text: The shop floor looks like a battlefield. A man is fighting a woman for the last light-up reindeer. You are the only staff member with a free pair of hands.

outcomes.text: I split them with a clipboard and a firm voice. The reindeer went to the first person who touched it.
It turned into a shouting match and security came. The reindeer ended up in pieces.
In the stockroom there was one, in a battered box. Both customers took it as a gift.
There wasn't one. I made something up about 'a new shipment'.
It ended in a draw. They left in opposite directions with nothing, and I felt weirdly satisfied.
Somebody filmed it. The video did the rounds. The store was mentioned in the comments.

title: Rush hour
text: The whole queue arrives at once, and the screens turn red. Six drive-through orders, four counter orders, and the fryer timer is going off.

outcomes.text: I flew through it. By the end I felt like I'd run a marathon, and I'd loved it.
I flew through it and burned a finger on a tray. Worth it.
Between us we cleared the screens in record time. A manager nodded at me.
I got in someone's way and knocked a tray of fries. We laughed.

choices.label: Hide in the stockroom for a minute

outcomes.text: I counted to sixty and came back calmer, ready.
I was caught. The shift manager's eyebrow said it all.

title: The milkshake machine
text: The milkshake machine has been broken for three weeks and a regular has just ordered one for the fourth time. 'It's my birthday,' she says.

outcomes.text: It took twenty minutes, a lot of ice cream and a tiny sparkler from the drawer. She cried.
It came out lumpy and she ate it anyway, with great ceremony.
She understood. We gave her a free sundae instead.
She left unhappy. The sundae was cold comfort.

choices.label: Fake it with a cup of soft-serve

outcomes.text: She noticed. She smiled and ate it, because she's kind.
She noticed. She wrote a review.

title: The speed target
text: The board says the line is twelve percent behind. Someone has turned up the scanner pace overnight, and nobody has said so.

outcomes.text: I hit the number. My lower back reminded me the next day.
I hit the number and dropped a box of glassware. It came out of my wages.

choices.label: Raise it at the team meeting

outcomes.text: Three others agreed. Management reluctantly eased the target. It felt a bit like winning.
I was labelled 'difficult'. My shifts got worse.
I did a safe, steady pace and nobody fired me. A small victory.
I was written up for being slow.

title: The forklift near-miss
text: A forklift reverses out of the aisle with no horn and no beeper. You are in its path, looking at your scanner.

outcomes.text: It missed me by a hand's breadth. Everyone in the building was very quiet afterwards.
It clipped my heel. A bruise and a story.
The driver stopped. Nothing happened. The safety lead cried a bit.
He didn't hear. A colleague shoved me out of the way.
They fixed it the same day. A rare win.
They said they would. They did not. I told the union.

title: Black ice at 4 a.m.
text: The road ahead is a perfect silver ribbon. The dashboard says minus three. The rig feels light, and then it feels very light.

choices.label: Ease off the throttle and steer gently

outcomes.text: The truck held. I stopped at the next services and sat for twenty minutes with my hands shaking.
It slid sideways, caught, and straightened. I stopped and said a long prayer to no one.
The back end swung. The trailer clipped a barrier and the load shifted. I was fine, the freight less so.
I stopped in the ditch. Nothing broke but my pride and the dispatcher's patience.

choices.label: Pull in and wait for the gritter

outcomes.text: I lost two hours and nobody minded. The gritter came and I followed it home.
Dispatch was furious about the delay. I'd do it again.

title: The hitchhiker
text: Midnight on a long empty road, and a figure stands in your headlights with a thumb out and a rucksack. Company policy is clear: no passengers.

outcomes.text: A student, trying to get home. She slept for most of it, and woke up to thank me. It cost me nothing.
A strange man, as it turned out. The twenty minutes felt like two hours. I put him down at a petrol station.
I watched her shrink in the mirror. I thought about her more than I should.
I called it in, later. A patrol car found her. She was fine.

choices.label: Stop and call the police for her

outcomes.text: A patrol car came; she was embarrassed but safe. I got a thank-you card.
She had been waiting for her brother, who showed up as I left. Slightly awkward.

title: What you find in the bins
text: In a bin outside the boardroom, under a pile of shredded paper, there is a clear envelope full of cash.

outcomes.text: It turned out to be the petty cash for an event. They gave me a bonus and a handshake I'll remember.
Nobody claimed it. After a month, the manager said I could have it. It paid the electricity bill for the year.
I spent it quickly, and guiltily. The envelope haunted me.
A camera had caught it. I was walked out by security.
A week later it was gone, and so was the person who had hidden it. I never found out.
I told a manager. They said 'thanks' and the envelope vanished. I don't know where.

title: The long night
text: Empty offices at night have their own rules. At 2 a.m. the senior partner is still at his desk, head down, shoulders shaking.

choices.label: Quietly leave a coffee on his desk

outcomes.text: He looked up and smiled. We never discussed it. He remembered my name at the Christmas party.
He didn't look up. The coffee was cold when I came back. Sometimes nothing happens.
He told me his wife had left. For ten minutes I wasn't the cleaner. I was a person.
He snapped at me. I felt foolish, but I'd do it again.
I did my job and he never knew. Sometimes that's the kindest thing.
He asked if I could be quieter. I could.

title: The 3 a.m. alarm
text: A motion alarm trips in the empty east wing at 3 a.m. The cameras show nothing at all, and your torch is flickering.

outcomes.text: A bird had got in through a vent. It looked at me with real disgust.
A homeless man was asleep in the stairwell. We chatted quietly. I let him stay until dawn.
Backup took forty minutes and found the bird. I got teased for weeks.
Backup found someone. It turned out to be a real break-in, and my call prevented the worst.
Nothing happened. A shift later, I realised the camera had been unplugged.
I saw a shadow. I never knew what it was.

title: The rowdy guest
text: At a late event, a man has had far too much and is arguing with the bar staff. He is twice your size and extremely sure he is in the right.

outcomes.text: I made him laugh, took his arm, and got him a taxi. He called me 'mate' and hugged me. A win.
He swung at me. I stepped back and the other guards came in.
Three of us escorted him out. A professional, smooth little operation.
It escalated. A glass broke and a report had to be filed.

choices.label: Let the bar staff handle it

outcomes.text: They did, thank goodness, in their own way.
They didn't. I was blamed afterwards for 'not being there'.

title: The VIP in the lobby
text: A man in an immaculate coat has been waiting for forty minutes for a meeting that no one seems to have in their diary. He is polite, and radiating pressure.

outcomes.text: It was the chief executive's wife's brother. A tangle, but I sorted it. He remembered me.
He was in the wrong building. I gave him a map and a coffee.
He left, fuming. Somebody got shouted at, and it wasn't me.
He was an investor. It was a very bad forty minutes for the firm.

choices.label: Escort him to the board room

outcomes.text: I knocked and entered. Awkward, but it turned out to be the right door.
It wasn't the right door. I have never felt as small.

title: A mislaid message
text: You wrote down a phone message on a yellow note and put it on the wrong desk. Nobody knows. It was from a client, and it said 'urgent'.

outcomes.text: The partner groaned, called the client, and fixed it. I got a lecture and a gentle pat on the shoulder.
It was too late. The client had gone elsewhere. I was not fired, to my surprise.

choices.label: Find it and slip it onto the right desk

outcomes.text: Smoothly done. The message was read, the problem was fixed, and no one knew.
A colleague saw and kept it to themselves, but now they had something on me.
The client called back, angrier. The firm blamed the phone system.
It was never found out. I never forgot.
